778.title: Where were you, Krishna?
778.hook: Draupadi tells her friend Krishna that even he failed her, and he hears every word
778.carry: sakhya: you can tell God everything
778.howItsDone: Devotees revere Krishna as God, and storytellers dwell on this forest meeting, where Draupadi pours out her grief to her friend; sakhya, loving God as a friend, is counted among the classic ways of Hindu devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, where a vessel from the sun fed every guest, and Draupadi ate last. Your line was surya: the sun who ripens food for all.

Chariots on a forest road. Word has reached Krishna's people that the Pandavas are in exile, and Krishna comes to find them. The cousins embrace. Then Draupadi speaks, and she doesn't make small talk. She tells him everything: the hall, being dragged in by her hair, the laughter, the husbands who sat silent. She weeps as she speaks. And under all of it is one question she doesn't quite need to say out loud. Where were you?
screen: `KRISHNA COMES TO THE FOREST.` → `DRAUPADI TELLS EVERYTHING.` → `WHERE WERE YOU?`

segments.voice: Draupadi doesn't tidy her grief. She names each wrong, in order, to the one person she trusts to hear it whole. In the epic's telling, she gives him four reasons he should protect her: they're family, her dignity, his power to help, and one more word worth holding onto, sakhya, their friendship. Then the hardest thing: she has no husband, no son, no brother, not even Krishna, because none of them protected her. Krishna, whom devotees worship as God, doesn't scold her. He makes her a promise: the women of those who wronged her will one day weep as she is weeping now. Then, turning to Yudhishthira, he answers the question underneath. Had I been in Dvaraka, I would have come to that game uninvited and stopped it. But he was away, fighting a king named Shalva, who had attacked his city. Draupadi speaks to Krishna as a friend, and in Hindu devotion that's a real way to love God. It's called sakhya: friendship with God. In the Bhagavata Purana, the boy Prahlada lists nine ways of devotion, and friendship is one of them; devotees often name Draupadi and Arjuna as its great examples. A friend can say the hard thing. So many Hindus feel free to bring God everything: grief, anger, even 'where were you?' Many teachers read the scene that way: devotion isn't only polite praise. Honest words, said to God and heard all the way through, are prayer too.
screen: `DRAUPADI NAMES EACH WRONG.` · `NOT EVEN YOU, KRISHNA.` · `I WAS FIGHTING SHALVA.` · then, large: `SAKHYA: GOD AS A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: If you have a home shrine, sit before it; if not, anywhere quiet will do. Tell God, Krishna, or the holy as you know it, one true thing you've been holding back: a hurt, a disappointment, a 'where were you'. Say it plainly, in your own words, the way Draupadi spoke to her friend. Then stay a few breaths and let yourself be heard. If you don't pray, say it to the quiet, or write it down, and let it be heard all the way through.
Vana. The forest of exile, where Draupadi tells her friend Krishna everything, and he hears it all.
Your line: sakhya: you can tell God everything. Draupadi did, and Krishna heard her to the end. Tomorrow: is forgiving always right? Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.

779.title: Forgive, or fight back?
779.hook: in the forest, Draupadi argues for might and Yudhishthira for kshama, forgiveness, and Prahlada's old answer weighs both
779.carry: kshama is strength, but dharma reads the hour
779.tomorrow: they were cheated. why keep the promise?
779.howItsDone: Teachers and commentators return to this forest debate between Draupadi and Yudhishthira when discussing anger, kshama (forgiveness) and right action, and Prahlada's answer to Bali, a time for each, is retold on its own as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, where Draupadi told her friend Krishna everything, and he heard her to the end. Your line was sakhya: you can tell God everything.

An evening in the forest, and a married couple is having a real argument. Draupadi looks at her husband in his bark clothes, sleeping on the ground, and she can't stand it. You were a king, she says. Your brothers are suffering. How is your anger not blazing? Yudhishthira doesn't storm out. He answers her, at length. And she answers back. The epic doesn't cut the scene short or tell us who won. It gives both of them the floor.
screen: `A COUPLE ARGUES IN THE FOREST.` → `WHY IS YOUR ANGER NOT BLAZING?` → `BOTH OF THEM GET THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Draupadi doesn't argue from feeling alone. She brings a story. Long ago, she says, the demon king Bali asked his grandfather Prahlada, the same Prahlada whose verdict Vidura told in the hall: which is better, forgiveness or might? Prahlada answered: neither one, always. Someone who forgives everything is treated with contempt, even by his own servants. Someone who never forgives makes enemies of everyone. There's a time for each, and wisdom is knowing which time it is. Now, says Draupadi, is the time for might. Yudhishthira answers with a different picture. Anger, he says, is the root of destruction; an angry person can't tell what should be said from what shouldn't. Forgiveness holds the world together. He calls it the strength of the strong. The word he praises is kshama: forgiveness, patience under wrong, and old Hindu lists of the marks of dharma include it. So who is right? Here's the teaching the scene leaves you with. Kshama is a real strength, not a weakness. But Prahlada adds the word that keeps it honest: time. Dharma isn't one rule for every moment; it reads the hour. Is the person sorry? Is this the first time? Would forgiving now protect anyone, or only let the harm go on? Draupadi isn't the hothead, and Yudhishthira isn't the saint. Both quote their tradition. That's why, in many Hindu homes, 'forgive' and 'stand up for yourself' can both be dharma. The wisdom is knowing which hour it is.
screen: `PRAHLADA: A TIME FOR EACH.` · `DRAUPADI: NOW IS THE TIME FOR MIGHT.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: KSHAMA IS STRENGTH.` · then, large: `DHARMA READS THE HOUR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one wrong someone did you, a medium one, not the biggest. Breathe in with Draupadi's question: is this a time for strength? Breathe out with Yudhishthira's: what would carrying this anger do to me? Then ask Prahlada's: what does this hour call for? If you pray, ask for kshama, and for the wisdom to know its time; if not, just let the three questions sit.

Your line: kshama is strength, but dharma reads the hour. Prahlada's answer was that each has its time. Tomorrow: they were cheated, so why keep the promise? That's day seven hundred seventy-nine.

780.title: A kingdom, or a word?
780.hook: Bhima argues for artha, wealth and power, and Yudhishthira answers that dharma comes first: he gave his word
780.tomorrow: who walks into a stuck camp with a plan?
780.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's insistence on keeping his word in exile is held up in Hindu storytelling as a picture of satya, truthfulness, and Bhima's speech on dharma, artha and kama is one of the epic's classic discussions of the aims of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, and the great argument. Draupadi asked for might, Yudhishthira for forgiveness. Your line was kshama is strength, but dharma reads the hour.

Bhima has been listening, and he's done waiting. He's built for action, strong and impatient. He's watched his brothers live on roots and his wife sleep on the ground, and he can't see the point. Our enemies cheated, he says. Why are we keeping faith with cheats? Let's go back and take what's ours. It's a fair question, and he asks it loudly.
screen: `BHIMA IS DONE WAITING.` → `WHY KEEP FAITH WITH CHEATS?` → `THE BROTHER WHO GAVE HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: Bhima's case is strong, and the epic lets him make it in full. The game was a trap. Every day in the forest, their enemies grow stronger. And he argues from the tradition itself. A life, he says, has aims: dharma, doing right; artha, wealth and power; kama, love and pleasure. You've held on to dharma alone, brother, and let the others starve. Yudhishthira hears him out, then answers with one thing. I gave my word. In the hall, in front of everyone, he agreed to the terms: the years in the forest, then a year in hiding. Breaking that promise now, he says, would be worse to him than losing the kingdom. The old word for what he's holding is satya: being someone whose word holds. Then he adds something practical: look who stands on the other side. Bhishma, Drona, Karna. We aren't ready. Here's the teaching. Hindu thought names the aims of a human life, the purusharthas: dharma, artha and kama, and later a fourth, moksha, release. None of them is shameful. Wanting success, money, a win: that's artha, an honored aim. But dharma comes first, and holds the others in shape. A kingdom taken by breaking your word would be artha without dharma. Bhima isn't wrong to want the kingdom back, and the epic doesn't mock him. Yudhishthira just won't buy it at that price.
screen: `BHIMA: DHARMA, ARTHA, KAMA.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: I GAVE MY WORD.` · `THE AIMS OF LIFE.` · then, large: `DHARMA LEADS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you want right now: a win, a raise, a grade, a place. It's allowed; artha is an honored aim. Now think of a promise that stands in its way. Let the Bhima in you ask, why not drop it, and breathe; then let the Yudhishthira in you ask, who would I be if I did, and breathe again. If you pray, offer both the wanting and the promise; if not, just hold them side by side.
Vana. The forest of exile, where Bhima argues for artha and Yudhishthira keeps the word he gave in the hall.
Your line: artha matters, but dharma leads. For Yudhishthira, a word that held was worth more than a kingdom. Tomorrow: who walks into a stuck camp with a plan? Day seven hundred eighty, done.

781.title: Vyasa sends Arjuna to the gods
781.hook: Vyasa walks into the stuck camp with a plan, not a miracle: Arjuna must climb to the gods for their weapons
781.carry: grace meets effort: pray, then climb
781.tomorrow: what does a holy man ask Arjuna to throw away?
781.howItsDone: Retellings of the Mahabharata mark Vyasa's visit as the turn in the forest years, when Arjuna leaves to seek divine weapons; Hindu teaching often pairs daiva, what the gods give, with human effort, and many Hindus pray before a task and then work at it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, where Bhima argued for artha, and Yudhishthira held to the word he gave. Your line was artha matters, but dharma leads.

An old sage walks into a stuck camp. Bhima wants them stronger, and soon. Yudhishthira won't break his word, and he knows how formidable the warriors on the other side are. The brothers are caught between impatience and patience. The visitor is Vyasa, grandfather of both the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and he has come with a way out.
screen: `STUCK BETWEEN IMPATIENCE AND PATIENCE.` → `VYASA WALKS IN.` → `WAITING BECOMES A PLAN.`

segments.voice: Vyasa takes Yudhishthira aside. I know what's in your heart, he says: the fear of Bhishma and Drona and Karna. So here's what to do. He gives Yudhishthira a sacred knowledge to teach to Arjuna, an inner discipline that will let him reach the gods. Arjuna must go, he says, and seek out the gods themselves, Indra and Rudra and the guardians of the world, and win their weapons through ascetic effort. That is how the Pandavas will be ready when the exile ends. Look at what Vyasa doesn't do. He doesn't bring the gods to the forest or end the exile with a miracle. The weapons are the gods' gifts, real grace, but Arjuna has to climb to them. Hindu teachers have long held two things together: daiva, what the gods and fate give, and purushakara, human effort. The epic weighs them more than once, and many teachers read its answer as both. It's why a Hindu student lights a lamp to Sarasvati, goddess of learning, before an exam, and still studies all week; why a family breaks a coconut before Ganesha to open a new shop, and then opens it at dawn. Prayer isn't a shortcut, and effort isn't the whole story. And notice the cost. Arjuna has to go alone. Yudhishthira teaches him what Vyasa taught, and Arjuna sets out, armed, toward the mountains of the north, with Draupadi's blessing on the road. Tomorrow we follow him up.
screen: `VYASA TAKES YUDHISHTHIRA ASIDE.` · `SEEK THE WEAPONS OF THE GODS.` · `DAIVA AND EFFORT.` · then, large: `NO MIRACLE. A CLIMB.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one task ahead of you, something you can't hurry. Many Hindus begin a task with a short prayer, to Ganesha who clears the way or to Sarasvati for learning, and then get to work. Try that shape now: breathe in and offer the task; breathe out and name one step you'll take today. If you don't pray, set the intention instead, and then name the step.

782.title: Throw away your bow
782.hook: on the mountain, a glowing ascetic tells Arjuna to throw away his bow, and Arjuna keeps to his own path
782.carry: svadharma: walk your own path, not another's
782.tomorrow: why would a warrior live on air?
782.howItsDone: Retellings of the Mahabharata follow Arjuna to the mountain, where Indra tests him in disguise before sending him to seek Shiva; Hindu teachers link the scene to svadharma, one's own duty, which Krishna teaches Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, became a base camp. Vyasa sent Arjuna to climb to the gods. Your line was grace meets effort: pray, then climb.

Stop. The word rings out across a mountain slope in the north, and Arjuna stops. He has walked a long way, bow in hand, quiver on his back, toward a peak the epic calls Indrakila. Under a tree sits an ascetic: thin, matted hair, glowing with the strength of long discipline. He looks at the armed young man and asks, more or less: what are you doing with those? This is a place of peace. The first test of Arjuna's austerities doesn't look like a test at all.
screen: `STOP.` → `AN ASCETIC UNDER A TREE.` → `WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH THOSE?`

segments.voice: The ascetic goes on. Here, he says, live peaceful seekers who have left anger behind. There's no need for weapons in this place. Throw away your bow. You've already reached a high state. He asks again and again. But Arjuna won't put the bow down. He won't leave his brothers waiting in the forest, he says, and go off to some peaceful world without the weapons he came for. Then the ascetic shows who he really is: Indra, king of the gods, and in the story Arjuna's own father. Pleased, he offers his son a boon. Arjuna asks for weapons. Indra answers: first, you must see Shiva, the three-eyed god who holds the trident. Then I'll give you mine. So the first test isn't whether he can give everything up. It's whether he'll stay on his own path when a holy one offers another. And the epic plants a seed here. Years later, at Kurukshetra, Arjuna himself will drop his bow and want to walk away, and Krishna will answer him in the Bhagavad Gita: better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's done well. That's svadharma: your own duty, fitted to who you are and where you stand. A hermit's peace is holy, and for the hermit it is dharma. But Arjuna has brothers waiting and a promise to keep. For him, laying the bow down here would mean walking someone else's path. The Gita's question isn't whose path is holier. It's whether you're on yours.
screen: `THROW AWAY YOUR BOW.` · `IT WAS INDRA ALL ALONG.` · `BETTER YOUR OWN DHARMA.` · then, large: `SVADHARMA: YOUR OWN PATH.`

segments.voice: Sit still and bring to mind the roles you hold right now: child, friend, student, worker, parent. Breathe in and name one; breathe out and ask, what is my dharma in this one, today? 783.title: A warrior living on air
783.hook: Arjuna fasts until he lives on air, the sages feel the heat of his tapas, and Shiva says he already knows Arjuna's heart

783.howItsDone: Tapas, disciplined austerity such as fasting, stillness and self-restraint, runs through Hindu stories and practice; many Hindus keep vratas, such as Monday fasts for Shiva, Ekadashi fasts for Vishnu and the Maha Shivaratri vigil, as offerings of devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's austerities began with a test. Indra, in disguise, told him to throw away his bow, and he kept to his own path. Your line was svadharma: walk your own path, not another's.

A warrior in grass clothes. That's what the sages on the mountain see when they look at the newcomer. Arjuna, prince and archer, has traded his royal dress for rags of grass and a deerskin, and taken up a staff. He's come to the foot of the Himalayas to do one thing: draw the attention of Shiva. And the way he sets about it is tapas, the slow, burning work of austerity.
screen: `A WARRIOR IN GRASS CLOTHES.` → `TO DRAW SHIVA'S ATTENTION.` → `THE BURNING WORK OF TAPAS.`

segments.voice: The epic describes it step by step. At first Arjuna eats fruit, but only every few nights. Then less often. Month by month he narrows his life, until he lives on air alone, standing on the tips of his toes with his arms raised. In this story, tapas burns, and the burning is real. The sages who live on the mountain feel it; smoke, in the epic's telling, seems to rise from the earth around him. Worried, they go to Shiva: who is this man, and what is he doing? Shiva's answer is calm. Don't worry. I know what's in Arjuna's heart. I know what he wants. Go back, and be at peace. Arjuna hasn't said a word to Shiva. His discipline has spoken for him. That's tapas, one of Hinduism's oldest ideas: discipline as a fire, offered to God. It's why Hindu homes still keep vratas, vows of fasting and restraint. Many keep Mondays for Shiva, fasting or eating simply until evening. Many fast on Ekadashi for Vishnu, or stay awake through the night of Maha Shivaratri. The point isn't to suffer, and it isn't to be seen. Shiva knew Arjuna's heart before Arjuna said a word. In a vrat, the fast is how the heart speaks back.
screen: `LESS FOOD, THEN ONLY AIR.` · `TAPAS GIVES OFF HEAT.` · `SHIVA ALREADY KNOWS.` · then, large: `TAPAS: DISCIPLINE OFFERED.`

segments.voice: Hindus who keep a vrat often begin with a sankalpa, a quiet intention. Try a small one now: choose one thing to go without today, a snack, a scroll, a complaint. Breathe in and name it; breathe out and offer it, to Shiva or to God as you know God. If you don't pray, offer it for someone you love. Then keep it quietly; no one else needs to know.

784.title: Shiva the hunter
784.hook: a boar charges, two arrows strike it at once, and Arjuna sneers at a mountain hunter who is Shiva
784.carry: the divine can come as the one you dismiss
784.tomorrow: how will Arjuna see who the hunter is?
784.howItsDone: The meeting of Arjuna and Shiva as a hunter is retold in Hindu storytelling, poetry and temple art, and Shiva in the guise of a Kirata is honored as a form of the god; stories of the divine arriving in disguise run all through Hindu tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's austerities burned so hot the sages went to Shiva, and Shiva said, I know what he wants. Your line was tapas: discipline offered to God, not shown.

Crashing through the trees, a boar. It's huge, and it's coming straight at Arjuna. The story tells us it's no ordinary animal: a demon named Muka has taken this shape to kill the man at prayer. Thin from fasting, Arjuna still moves fast. He grabs his bow, nocks an arrow and draws. And at that very moment, someone else is drawing too: a hunter, a Kirata, one of the mountain people, with a woman at his side and a crowd behind him. Two archers. One boar.
screen: `A BOAR CRASHES THROUGH THE TREES.` → `ARJUNA DRAWS HIS BOW.` → `SO DOES A HUNTER.`

segments.voice: The listener knows something Arjuna doesn't. The hunter is Shiva, come down the mountain in disguise, and the woman beside him is his consort Uma, also disguised. Stop, the hunter calls. I aimed at that boar first. Arjuna ignores him and shoots. So does the hunter. Both arrows strike at the same instant, and the boar falls dead, in its own demon shape again. Arjuna is furious. Who are you, he demands? Why did you shoot the game I had already marked? That breaks the rules of the hunt. I'll take your life for it. The hunter isn't impressed. This forest is our home, he says. I claimed that boar first. Look at the turn. After all that discipline, the first stranger Arjuna meets makes him furious in seconds, and he speaks to him like a nobody from the hills. And the nobody is Shiva. This is one of the deep patterns of Hindu storytelling: God comes in disguise, as a hunter, a beggar, a guest at the door. Shiva as the Kirata, the hunter, is honored as one of his forms, and Hindu belief holds that the divine can take any form it chooses. An old Upanishad puts it in three words many Hindu children learn: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be God to you. That's part of why so many Hindus meet a stranger with folded hands. Arjuna's austerities have made him strong. They haven't yet made him see. And he's about to pick a fight with the very god he came to find.
screen: `THE HUNTER IS SHIVA IN DISGUISE.` · `ARJUNA: WHO ARE YOU?` · `GOD COMES IN DISGUISE.` · then, large: `GOD IN THE ONE YOU DISMISS.`

As you breathe out, fold your hands, the old Hindu greeting, namaste: I bow to you. If you pray, ask to see the holy in that person; if not, just wish them well.
